4051.tone: The source does not analyse tone in the modern varieties; its review of earlier proposals (§3, Cuadro 2 p. 56 with fn. 5, p. 57) places contrastive tone on long vowels in Yucatec only ('la emergencia de contraste tonal (presente en yucateco)'), lists Southern Lacandon vowels (after Herrera 2014) as short / long / laryngealised with no tonal series, and reports the Fisher (1976) / Hofling (2015) scenario of loss of proto-Yucatecan tone in Lacandon, Mopan and Itzaj. Bennett 2016 (p. 501, second-hand) reports that Southern Lacandon 'appears to have lexical tone' per an unpublished Canger 1995 ms., and Spanish Wikipedia, citing Hofling 2017 (not opened here), says Southern Lacandon distinguishes high and low lexical tone on long vowels like Yucatec; that claim is not supported by this article and remains unverified.

4052.tone: Lachixío has phonemic tone alongside stress. Sicoli 2010: 532-533 (first-hand, by the 2007 dissertation author; open PDF; key pp. 552-553): 'In the grammatical system of Lachixío Zapotec, low tone is used to indicate the imperative mood (Sicoli 2007:97).'... 'Breathy voice also emerges in the Lachixío phonological system from low tone in morphophonological environments, where low tones "pile up" in adjacency. In example (8) the phonemic low tone is marked by /L/, phonetic low tone by grave accent. (8) //e= L+koko+L// ek#òkkò# ‘corn dough (masa)’'; key: '` low tone ´ high tone'. Sicoli 2010 does not discuss stress placement (its only 'stress' token is non-technical). tn.quote: El zapoteco difiere del español en que cada sílaba tiene un tono particular, y a veces la única diferencia que existe en la pronunciación de dos palabras radica en el tono. ... En el diccionario los tonos están indicados con números del uno al cuatro, que significan los siguientes tonos: 1 = tono ascendente 2 = tono alto 3 = tono medio 4 = tono bajo En esta gramática, escribimos los números de los tonos solamente cuando es necesario para distinguir entre dos o más palabras con las mismas letras. Como en español, el zapoteco tiene contraste entre palabras por la posición de la sílaba tónica.
tn.translation: Zapotec differs from Spanish in that each syllable has a particular tone, and sometimes the only difference in the pronunciation of two words lies in the tone. ... In the dictionary the tones are indicated with numbers from one to four, which mean the following tones: 1 = rising tone 2 = high tone 3 = mid tone 4 = low tone In this grammar we write the tone numbers only when it is necessary to distinguish two or more words with the same letters. As in Spanish, Zapotec has contrast between words by the position of the stressed syllable.
tn.cite: Persons, David D., Cheryl A. Black & Jan A. Persons (2009). Gramática de zapoteco de Lachixío. México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. vii+104 pp.
tn.note: ILV grammar: four tones (rising, high, mid, low), one per syllable, written as numbers only where needed, plus a stress contrast. Sicoli (2007, 2016) writes H and L only, contours as sequences.

In these the first syllable generally has the stress. Examples: chu'mig, well; rkang'lag, limb; lag'shub, glove; nyinlam, day's march; tang'rag, thanks. 4058.heavy: No weight-based stress rule is stated. The shift schema //CV́C(h)V(V)CV// -> /CVC(h)V́VCV/, //CV́C(h)VCCV// -> /CVC(h)V́(V)CCV/ applies only when the stressed first syllable is short and open and a third syllable follows; a closed first syllable (tállahmi, jólkati, kaʔáppi) blocks it, and the landing syllable is lengthened when open. 4058.prule: Stress is a property of roots, not of a position in the word: roots are stressed (strong) or unstressed (weak), affixes never bear stress, and a word carries at most one stressed root (some words carry none). A canon-conditioned morphophonemic shift then moves the root's stress from its first to its second syllable whenever the word has the shape //CV́C(h)V(V)CV// or //CV́C(h)VCCV// (tawháalak 'worker', ʔupúutak 'swimmer', kaníini 'with me', howónni 'chair'); elsewhere (heavy first syllable: tállahmi, jólkati, kaʔáppi; disyllables: káluk, kíik) no shift.

4069.tone: Described as a tone language (Summary p. 67: 'a tone language with a two-way distinction between H (high) and L (low)'). System = register (H/L) at the word-initial position + optional accent nucleus between syllables 1 and 2; TBU = first two syllables, rest atonal. On stress the source is explicitly agnostic: 'no linguistic realisation supports either the existence or non-existence of stress on a single syllable' (p. 79); the Tibetic stress-accent framework (Caplow 2016a, 2016b) is said not to have been applied to Lamo. The authors liken the system to Kansai (Keihan) Japanese and avoid the label 'pitch accent', which they attribute to Ikeda (2002) and Ding (2001) for Darmdo Minyag and Prinmi (p. 81). A reviewer could code this as pitch-accent-like; either way it falls under tone or pitch accent.

4072.dq: Dans la grande majorité des cas, l’accent se place sur la première syllabe du thème ou du radical. Il remplit ainsi un rôle démarcatif, en permettant aux interlocuteurs de saisir les frontières entre les mots. (Dunham 2001: 102) — and §5.1.2.4 contrasts the single accent domain of compounds (,mʊntʊ mʊ'ki) with the two word accents of a qualifying phrase (kɪ'paŋga kɪ'lʊmɛ).

4072.prule: Dunham 2001 (the only dedicated description of the accent, §5.1 pp. 99–103, with duration measurements): a demarcative word accent (tense articulation, higher amplitude, markedly longer syllable; ma-'bahɪra: ba 500–550 ms vs 240–340 ms elsewhere) falls on the first syllable of the stem/radical, i.e. the syllable after the class prefix (absolute initial when the prefix is amalgamated or absent; on the second prefix when there are two) — anchored to the stem boundary, not computable from syllable count. Stegen 2002 (a derivational-morphology paper) describes a H/L mora-tone system and, in one subordinate clause (p. 137), says the penultimate 'as in many Bantu languages, normally receives stress'; but his only stress-marked data (p. 131 ex. 2: kʊlʊ́'máɲa, kʊ'lʊ́manya) put the stress on the root-initial syllable of both verbs — in kʊ'lʊ́manya (kʊ.lʊ́.ma.nya) on the antepenult — i.e. where Dunham's rule puts it and not on the penult. The two sources therefore agree on the data (stem/root-initial) and differ only between Dunham's stated rule and Stegen's hedged generic-Bantu aside, which coincide for the common CV-prefix + disyllabic-stem word.
4072.srule: Only in compounds and reduplicated stems (Dunham 2001 §5.1.2.4): a secondary accent, weaker than the main accent, on the absolute initial of the first term / first copy, with the main accent on the stem-initial syllable of the second component (mʊntʊ mʊ'ki 'woman'; i-,findu'findu 'tonsil',tina'tina 'cut well!'); simplex words carry a single stem-initial accent and no secondary accent is described for them; a qualifying phrase has two main accents (kɪ'paŋga kɪ'lʊmɛ).

4072.tone: Stegen 2002 §1.1 (pp. 131–134): H and L tones, mora TBU (short vowels H/L, long vowels H/L/rising/falling), phrase-final H deletion (which he says explains why the literature, e.g. Guthrie, Nurse 1999, portrays Rangi as having lost tone), nouns fully tonally distinctive (mukúvu 'navel' vs mukúlu 'father-in-law' type pairs), verbs one H on the antepenultimate stem mora spreading leftward, grammatical tone (imperative, distant past vs past habitual distinguished by tone only); fn. 5: Kolo dialect has lexical verb-tone minimal pairs that Haubi, Kondoa and Mondo lack. Gibson 2012 §2.2.3 pp. 25–26 restates this ('Rangi is a two-tone language exhibiting high and low tones'); Stegen 2011 §1.3.1 marks H tone in the orthography. Dunham 2001 §5.4 p. 108: regularities indicate 'une survivance, au moins, d’un système tonal' (independent prefixes L, locative -i H) but she could not extract a tone system with Swahili-dominant Kondoa-town speakers and calls for fieldwork outside Kondoa; Dunham 2004 fn. 3: tonal distinctions 'so restricted' that tone is not marked.

tn.quote: In Rangi, there are high and low tones (marked with acute accent and unmarked, respectively). As shown in Table 3, short vowels occur with high or low tone whereas long vowels occur with high, low, rising or falling tone. This is an indication of the fact that the mora, and not the syllable, is the tone bearing unit in Rangi. A phrase-final H tone deletion rule operates in Rangi. … On verbs, lexical tone distinctions seem to have been lost. … Every verbal stem receives one H tone which, as shown in (5), is assigned to the ante-penultimate stem mora and spreading to any preceding stem morae.
tn.cite: Stegen, Oliver. 2002. Derivational processes in Rangi. Studies in African Linguistics 31(1/2): 129–153.
tn.note: Two tones, high and low, borne by the mora (long vowels may surface rising or falling); nouns lexically distinctive, verbs take one assigned H; final H deleted phrase-finally; separate word stress.

4075.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable, counted from the right edge of the word over vowels (each vowel is a syllable nucleus; a like-vowel sequence counts as two, so in careful speech stress lands on the second half of a geminate vowel: kaancu [kaˈanʧu], paraaso [ˌparaˈaso]). quantity-insensitive: no closed-syllable or long-vowel attraction is stated; suffixation re-places primary stress on the new penult (kaʔoŋkowulu [kaˌʔoŋkoˈβulu] vs kaʔoŋkowuluno [kaˌʔoŋkoβuˈluno]).

4076.dq: Ударение в именных частях речи и в наречиях падает на последний слог слова: estāré 'звезда', berā́ 'брат', esbí 'белый', panjā́ 'пятьдесят', hamišák 'всегда'.
4076.dloc: Rastorgueva 1999 p. 158, section 'Фонетические сведения', second paragraph ('Ударение в именных частях речи...'); belt article 'Семнана полосы диалекты' pp. 149-150; Christensen 1935 'Accentuation' §§ 35-39, pp. 34-35.
4076.prule: Word stress on the final syllable of the word in the nominal parts of speech (nouns, adjectives, pronouns, numerals) and adverbs: estāré 'star', berā́ 'brother', esbí 'white', panjā́ 'fifty', hamišák 'always'. Syllable weight is never mentioned; the pattern is the Persian type (Christensen § 35: 'les deux patois suivent en général les mêmes règles que le persan'). The ezafe -e and the postposed indefinite/unit marker -i are enclitic and do not take stress, so the stress stays on the last syllable of the host (vā́y-e saxt, váxt-i). The belt article pp. 149-150 states the same categorical rule for all four Semnan-belt dialects with Lasgerdi examples šišé 'bottle', šišón 'bottles'.
4076.srule: In verb forms with a derivational prefix the main stress is on the prefix and a secondary stress on the personal ending (débastèym 'I tied', hā́kardamùn 'we did'); forms with stressed be- and negative na- are likewise transcribed with a secondary mark on the ending (bébordèm, nábarà, ānámedàš). No secondary stress is mentioned for nominals or adverbs. Christensen 1935 § 37: with a prefix the ending carries a secondary accent 'ordinairement en sourkhéï, et quelquefois en lâsguerdï', sometimes almost as strong as the prefix accent.
